ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in Figure A, the mass of the laptop is $m$. Its cooling stand is generally equipped with four notches to adjust the angle. A student placed the laptop on the cooling stand and adjusted it to notch 4 (as indicated by the solid line in Figure B). When the angle between the inclined surface of the cooling stand and the horizontal direction is $\alpha$, the laptop remains stationary on the inclined surface of the cooling stand. The gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. The magnitude of the elastic force and the frictional force acting on the computer at this moment.
2. When adjusted to position 1 (as shown by the dashed line in Figure B), the inclination angle of the heat dissipation base increases to θ (θ > α). At this point, a gentle push causes the laptop to slide down the inclined surface of the heat dissipation base at a constant speed. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the laptop and the inclined surface of the heat dissipation base?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: Figure A shows a laptop cooling stand with four adjustment notches labeled 1, 2, 3, 4. Figure B shows the stand/laptop as an inclined plane: the solid-line position corresponds to notch 4 and makes angle α with the horizontal; a dashed position near notch 1 is steeper and corresponds to angle θ, with θ > α. Reasoning: For part 1, model the laptop as a block on an incline of angle α. Its weight mg resolves into a component perpendicular to the plane, mg cos α, and a component parallel to the plane down the slope, mg sin α. Since the laptop is stationary, the net force perpendicular to the plane is zero, so the elastic/normal force is N = mg cos α. The net force along the plane is also zero, so static friction acts up the plane with magnitude f = mg sin α. For part 2, at the steeper angle θ the laptop slides down at constant speed, so acceleration is zero. Perpendicular to the plane, N = mg cos θ. Along the plane, gravity's downslope component mg sin θ is balanced by kinetic friction μ_k N upslope. Thus μ_k mg cos θ = mg sin θ, so μ_k = tan θ.
